sections.html:
Hamilton County lies directly north of Indianapolis, with Noblesville as the county seat. Carmel is the largest city, followed by Fishers and Noblesville, and Arcadia, Atlanta, Cicero, Sheridan and Westfield are towns. The county has nine townships, and Clay Township matches the boundaries of Carmel.

Growth has been steady. Population was 182,740 in 2000, 274,569 in 2010 and 347,467 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 387,036. The northern part is still largely farmland, while suburban development has spread north from Indianapolis. Geist and Morse reservoirs add waterfront homes to the mix, and older areas near downtown Noblesville and Carmel sit beside new construction, so condition varies from block to block.

The treasurer collects payments, the auditor handles deductions and the tax sale, and the assessor values property. The treasurer and auditor work from the Historic Courthouse in downtown Noblesville.

OfficeLocation and contact
Treasurer33 N 9th Street, Suite 112, Noblesville; 317-776-9620; Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Auditor deductions desk33 N 9th Street, first floor, southwest corner; 317-770-4412
Auditor tax sale desk33 N 9th Street, Suite 214; tax.sale@hamiltoncounty.in.gov

You can pay online, by mail, in person or at listed banks. Credit cards work only online. Mail needs a postmark on or before the due date, and a postage meter date does not count. A drop box sits at the west doors of the Historic Courthouse, and anything left after midnight on the deadline counts as late. Banks that take payments include BMO Bank, Community First Bank of Indiana, Farmers Bank, First Farmers Bank, Horizon Bank, Merchants Bank of Indiana and Star Financial Bank. Bring the tax statement.

The county also offers e-billing and an online portal where owners can see statements, payments, assessed values and property record cards.

sections.h2: How Hamilton County assesses so many homes
sections.html:
Hamilton County had 148,707 parcels at the end of 2024, and the assessor's office does most of the valuation work in house. During 2024, 3,721 new parcels were created from 134 new plats and 75 splits, and 2,588 of them carried new construction. Plats and combinations removed 150 parcels. A land order took effect January 1, 2025.

For 2025, the state's new cost tables, adjusted by a Verified Economic Modifier, significantly affected improvement values. Smaller neighborhoods with little sales data had lagged the market, so some saw large increases, while larger neighborhoods saw little change. The county expected 2025 residential assessments to rise. MIBOR statistics show a 7.2% increase in median single-family sale price from January 2024 to January 2025.

The 2024 cyclical phase reviewed residential property in Washington Township and parts of Noblesville and Fall Creek townships, along with agricultural land in White River, Wayne and Delaware townships. Reviewed commercial neighborhoods included hotels, car dealerships, self-storage and the major downtown redevelopment. When a permit is pulled for an addition or remodel, the property is inspected. Transitional areas where older homes are replaced by new construction may get their own neighborhoods.

File a Form 130 with the assessor, one per parcel, by June 15. Which year that falls in depends on whether the Form 11 notice was mailed before May 1. The assessor holds an informal meeting, and then the county appeals board must hold a hearing within 180 days, with 30 days of written notice. A $50 penalty can apply for a no-show with no continuance. If you disagree with the result, Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

The state caps the bill at 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for nonresidential and personal property. The 1% cap requires the homestead deduction.

The county's deduction page lists the standard homestead deduction, the over 65 credit, the blind and disabled credit and recorded land contract benefits. File by January 15 to affect the next bill. Once approved, you generally do not reapply unless you change the deed, marry or change the property's use. A third-party vendor, Tax Management Associates, may mail letters asking homeowners to clarify eligibility, and the county confirms those letters are legitimate.

sections.h2: The tax sale and your parcel
sections.html:
The auditor runs the county's real property tax sale each year at 33 North 9th Street, in the Second Floor Historic Courtroom, and payments go to the treasurer. The 2026 sale was set for 10 a.m. on a Thursday in October. Call the auditor's tax sale desk for the next date.

  • To pull a parcel from the sale, pay the full amount to the treasurer by noon the day before the sale, in cash, cashier's check or money order.
  • The property list is updated each Friday, normally by noon, in the two months before the sale.
  • An owner has three years after a sale to claim surplus funds if the parcel sold for more than the debt.

Penalties build before a sale. A late payment takes 5% if made within 30 days and no earlier delinquency exists, and 10% in other cases. An extra 10% of unpaid tax is added after later installment dates.

If you sell through a title company, the unpaid amount comes out of your proceeds at closing, so a delinquent parcel does not block a sale. Work through the same short list each time.

  1. Call the treasurer at 317-776-9620 for the full balance, including penalties.
  2. Check the county's online portal for statements, payments, assessed values and property record cards, and fix anything that looks wrong before you list.
  3. If your parcel is on the sale list, decide whether to pay it off now or close before the sale. Remember the noon cutoff the day before.
  4. Tell the title company about the balance when you open the file.

A cash buyer can often close quickly and take the house in its current condition, which is useful when the tax sale is close. The balance still comes out of the proceeds. If the house has flood damage, expect buyers to ask for photos, insurance claims and repair records, and check your coverage first because standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood damage.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to in Hamilton County?
faqs.a: You pay the Hamilton County Treasurer at 33 N 9th Street, Suite 112 in Noblesville, or online. The phone number is 317-776-9620. Credit cards are accepted online only.

faqs.q: Can I sell a flood-damaged house in Hamilton County?
faqs.a: Yes. Many owners sell as-is after a flood. Buyers will ask for photos, insurance claims and repair records, and standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood damage, so check your coverage first.

faqs.q: When is the appeal deadline in Hamilton County?
faqs.a: June 15, filed on Form 130 with the county assessor. The year depends on whether the Form 11 notice came before or after May 1.

faqs.q: What if my Hamilton County parcel is on the tax sale list?
faqs.a: You can remove it by paying the full balance to the treasurer by noon the day before the sale, using certified funds. The list is searchable on the county site and updated on Fridays.

faqs.q: Do I lose my homestead deduction when I sell?
faqs.a: The deduction belongs to the owner who files for it, so the buyer files a new application. The county asks owners to file by January 15 to affect the next bill, and you generally do not reapply unless the deed, marital status or use changes.
